title: LambdaHealth QBR - Unit economics + optimization review
customer_attendees: Dr. Priya Nair (Head of Clinical AI)
summary: Quarterly business review focused on blended $/1M output tokens, recent cost movements, and optimization levers (KV/prefix cache, batching, quantization profiles, and routing). Redwood walked through the internal Unit Economics dashboard (time series + drilldowns by model, region, tier) to explain an apparent cost spike that was largely a metering parity fix for streaming plus a temporary cache hit-rate drop. Agreed on an optimization plan: enable Redwood-recommended batching settings for two high-volume routes, expand prefix caching for repeated system prompts, and test an int8 quantization profile for one summarization workload with quality guardrails. Finance requested a monthly reconciliation snapshot and clearer annotation when methodology/rate-card changes occur.
topics: Q4 and QTD usage recap (tokens, throughput, top routes)
Blended $/1M output tokens: definition and what changed in January
Drilldowns: model/version, region (us-east vs eu-west), and workload mix
Cache hit rate + batching efficiency signals and how they map to cost
Quantization profiles: candidate workloads + quality guardrails
Reconciliation expectations vs invoice totals; timing/day-boundaries
Next quarter plan: targets, reporting cadence, and stakeholders
action_items: Redwood (Nadia Rahman) - Share a short write-up explaining the streaming output-token metering parity fix and how it affects historical comparisons (include dates + dashboard annotation guidance) - Due 2025-02-10
Redwood (Logan Wright) - Send LambdaHealth a monthly unit-econ reconciliation snapshot (dashboard aggregate vs billing totals) for Feb close - Due 2025-03-05
Redwood (Aditya Rao) - Propose recommended batching configuration for LH-prod 'clinical-chat' and 'claim-summarize' routes (include expected $/1M and latency impact ranges) - Due 2025-02-14
LambdaHealth (Miguel Alvarez) - Provide a sample set of 200 prompts + expected outputs for summarization to use as a quantization quality gate - Due 2025-02-14
LambdaHealth (Jenna Park) - Confirm internal reporting timezone/day boundary for Finance (PST vs UTC) to align the monthly snapshot - Due 2025-02-12
Redwood (Allison Grant) - Add LambdaHealth-specific dashboard alerts/checks for sudden token drops (streaming/non-streaming parity) and share alert contact emails - Due 2025-02-21
next_steps: Redwood to send recap email with annotated screenshots of the unit economics drilldowns (model/region/tier) and the Jan change explanation.
Schedule a 30-min technical working session to implement batching + cache recommendations (week of Feb 17).
Run a 1-week A/B: baseline vs int8 quantization profile on summarization with agreed quality thresholds; review results in early March.
Start monthly Finance reconciliation snapshot (dashboard vs billing) starting Feb close.
transcript:
LambdaHealth QBR - Unit economics + optimization review
Recorded: 2025-02-06 18:00 UTC
Duration: 52 min
Attendees (Redwood): Aditya Rao, Logan Wright, Nadia Rahman, Allison Grant
Attendees (LambdaHealth): Sarah Kim, Dr. Priya Nair, Miguel Alvarez, Jenna Park


[00:00] Aditya Rao: Cool. I think we’re all on. Um, thanks everyone for making time. This is our QBR for LambdaHealth. We wanted to focus pretty heavily on unit economics because you all flagged that January looked weird.

[00:12] Sarah Kim: Yeah, “weird” is a polite way to say it. Our dashboard on our side showed cost per output token jumped and we couldn’t tell if it was region mix or model change or like, you know, something broke.

[00:24] Jenna Park: And Finance asked me twice this week if we’re going to blow the quarter because of “GPU price increases.” Which I don’t think is true, but I need a clean narrative.

[00:34] Aditya Rao: Totally. So plan: quick recap of Q4/QTD usage, then we’ll go into Redwood’s internal Unit Economics dashboard and show the drilldowns: model, region, and customer tier. You’re on Dedicated with us for most of prod, plus some hosted burst, so we’ll call that out.

[00:49] Dr. Priya Nair: Just to frame, our clinical assistant is stable, but the claims summarization workflow increased volume. We also turned on streaming for some experiences.

[01:01] Miguel Alvarez: Yeah, we flipped streaming on for the chat UI around Jan 9.

[01:06] Aditya Rao: Great, that’s actually relevant. Okay, I’m sharing screen.

[01:13] Logan Wright: I’ll also caveat: the dashboard we’re showing is internal, but we can share snapshots and the methodology. It’s the same metric our Finance team signs off for blended dollars per 1M output tokens.

[01:24] Sarah Kim: Fine, as long as we can reconcile to invoices within some tolerance.

[01:29] Aditya Rao: Yep.

[01:31] (screen share) Aditya Rao: So this is the overview page. Filters at top: time range, model, region, tier. I’m selecting last 60 days. Tier: Dedicated + Hosted burst.

[01:45] Aditya Rao: The headline metric: blended $/1M output tokens. In early Jan it looks like it rises. But, and this is important, part of that is a metering parity fix where streaming output tokens were under-counted before.

[02:03] Jenna Park: Wait. Under-counted tokens would make $ per token look… higher? Or lower?

[02:08] Nadia Rahman: Under-counted output tokens makes the denominator too small, so it makes dollars per 1M output tokens look higher than reality. When we fixed it, the token counts went up, so cost per 1M should go down—unless other stuff changed at the same time.

[02:24] Sarah Kim: But we saw a spike up, not down.

[02:27] Nadia Rahman: Right, and that’s why the time alignment matters. The fix landed in two phases: first we started counting streaming output tokens correctly for one path, then we normalized region mapping and there was a brief period where some traffic got attributed to “unknown region” and dropped out of a couple views. It made the blended series look jumpy for a few days.

[02:46] Allison Grant: Also, on your side, you turned on streaming, which changed the mix of code paths. The bug was specifically in streaming token emission from the gateway.

[02:56] Miguel Alvarez: Yeah, that tracks. We were seeing missing output token fields in some logs.

[03:01] Aditya Rao: Let’s make it concrete. I’m clicking “show contributing signals.” See here: output tokens, request count, cache hit rate, batching efficiency, and streaming flag distribution.

[03:13] Aditya Rao: Around Jan 9, streaming share goes from basically 0 to, like, 65% for your chat route. At the same time, cache hit rate dips.

[03:25] Dr. Priya Nair: Why would streaming affect cache?

[03:28] Aditya Rao: Streaming itself doesn’t. But the rollout coincided with a prompt template change on your side—more variability in the system prompt can reduce prefix cache hits. Miguel, did you change the system prompt or tool schema around then?

[03:42] Miguel Alvarez: Uh, we added a disclaimer and we changed the tool-call JSON schema slightly. Also added patient context block. So yeah, it changed.

[03:52] Aditya Rao: That would do it.

[03:54] Sarah Kim: Can you show us by region? Because we also routed more EU traffic to eu-west.

[04:01] Aditya Rao: Yep. Switching group-by to region. So: us-east, eu-west. Your blended $/1M is higher in eu-west by ~18% in this period.

[04:13] Jenna Park: Is that your GPU cost rate card being higher in EU?

[04:16] Logan Wright: Exactly. GPU hourly costs + some overhead differ by region. The dashboard uses a Finance-owned rate card. We can share the high level rates (not provider contract details), but the direction is: EU is more expensive.

[04:31] Sarah Kim: Okay, but is our workload less efficient in EU? Like lower batching or cache?

[04:36] Aditya Rao: Good question. Clicking eu-west and comparing. In eu-west, average output length is a bit higher—like 8-10%—and batching efficiency is slightly worse because concurrency is lower.

[04:50] Miguel Alvarez: That’s because EU traffic is smaller and more spiky. It never fills batches.

[04:56] Aditya Rao: Exactly. So two levers: (1) adjust autoscaling and min replicas to allow better continuous batching, and (2) consider routing EU low-latency workloads to us-east if compliance allows, but I know for you it doesn’t for some data.

[05:12] Dr. Priya Nair: For patient data, we’re strict. It stays in-region.

[05:15] Aditya Rao: Got it.

[05:17] Jenna Park: Back to the January “spike.” What’s the clean explanation I can tell Finance?

[05:22] Logan Wright: I’d phrase it as: (a) product change increased EU share and output length; (b) prompt changes reduced cache hit rate; (c) Redwood fixed streaming token metering, which changed how the metric is measured and removed an undercount. The “spike” is mostly measurement + mix, not an underlying GPU cost jump.

[05:42] Jenna Park: Okay. But I need that in writing with dates.

[05:46] Nadia Rahman: We can send a short note with the exact deploy window and how to compare pre/post. We should annotate that period on the chart.

[05:55] Aditya Rao: We’ll do that.

[05:57] Sarah Kim: Can we drill down by model? We switched from Llama 3.1 70B to… I think 70B-instruct v2? I’m not sure what you call it.

[06:07] Aditya Rao: Yep. In the dashboard the model identifier is a bit ugly. Here it’s “llama-3.1-70b-instruct” and version tag. You moved from v2024-12-18 to v2025-01-08.

[06:20] Miguel Alvarez: That’s the one that improved factuality.

[06:23] Dr. Priya Nair: Yes, fewer hallucinations on clinical codes.

[06:27] Aditya Rao: Great. That version has slightly higher prefill cost for long contexts. Your prefill/decode ratio increased because you started sending longer patient context blocks. Not huge, but it shows up.

[06:41] Sarah Kim: So longer context equals more expensive per output token even if output length is constant.

[06:46] Aditya Rao: Exactly. Because we’re normalizing by output tokens, but prefill compute is real. That’s why we also track prefill/decode ratio and average input tokens.

[06:57] Jenna Park: Wait, the KPI is per output tokens only. Isn’t that misleading if input grows?

[07:04] Logan Wright: It can be if you don’t look at the drivers. Finance wanted output-token normalization because it’s closest to “value delivered” for many apps. But the dashboard intentionally surfaces input and prefill/decode so you can interpret shifts.

[07:19] Sarah Kim: Okay.

[07:20] Aditya Rao: Now, optimization levers. First: caching. Your prefix cache hit rate dropped from ~34% to ~19% after the prompt change.

[07:31] Miguel Alvarez: That sounds right. We made the system prompt dynamic by department.

[07:37] Aditya Rao: Recommendation: keep the first N tokens stable across departments, and move the variable part later, or use a template key so we can cache prefixes effectively. Our runtime can cache based on prefix tokens; it’s sensitive to early variability.

[07:55] Dr. Priya Nair: But we need the disclaimer early.

[07:58] Aditya Rao: We can keep the disclaimer early, just keep it identical. The department-specific content can go later.

[08:06] Sarah Kim: That’s feasible.

[08:08] Aditya Rao: Second lever: batching. In eu-west your batching efficiency is around 0.62 vs 0.78 in us-east.

[08:18] Miguel Alvarez: What does 0.62 mean exactly?

[08:21] Logan Wright: It’s basically utilization of the continuous batch window. 1.0 would mean you’re consistently filling the target batch size. Lower means you’re running more “thin” batches.

[08:33] Miguel Alvarez: Is that something we control?

[08:36] Aditya Rao: Some of it you do via concurrency and request patterns; some we control via runtime config. For Dedicated, we can tune the batching window and max batch tokens by route. We can also adjust min capacity so spikes don’t cause cold starts that fragment batching.

[08:54] Jenna Park: Does increasing min capacity raise cost though?

[08:57] Aditya Rao: It can, yes. But it can reduce per-token cost if it materially improves utilization. We’d model it.

[09:06] Sarah Kim: I’d rather pay a bit more predictable fixed if it stops the per-token volatility.

[09:12] Aditya Rao: Makes sense.

[09:14] Allison Grant: We can set alerting on sudden changes too, so you’re not discovering it at the end of the month.

[09:22] Sarah Kim: Please.

[09:24] Aditya Rao: Third lever: quantization profiles. For summarization workloads, int8 can reduce cost per token. But we need quality guardrails.

[09:34] Dr. Priya Nair: We’re open to it for claims summary, not for clinical assistant responses.

[09:40] Aditya Rao: Perfect separation.

[09:42] Miguel Alvarez: What do you need from us for the guardrails?

[09:46] Aditya Rao: A small eval set: representative prompts and expected outputs or scoring rubric. We can do a side-by-side for one week.

[09:55] Dr. Priya Nair: We can provide a labeled set, but it can’t include PHI.

[10:00] Sarah Kim: We can scrub it.

[10:02] Aditya Rao: Great.

[10:04] Jenna Park: And how does this show up in the cost dashboard? Like, will it show “quant profile int8”?

[10:10] Logan Wright: Yes. Quantization profile is a first-class dimension. We also guard against weird values so it doesn’t explode metrics cardinality.

[10:21] Sarah Kim: Good.

[10:23] Aditya Rao: Let’s also address reconciliation. Jenna, you asked for recon to invoice.

[10:29] Jenna Park: Yes. We need a monthly snapshot that lines up with what you bill us.

[10:34] Logan Wright: The dashboard metric is “blended,” meaning it includes allocated infra cost for Dedicated capacity plus shared overhead based on usage. Billing is slightly different because of contract structure and timing. But we built a reconciliation report that compares aggregates to billing totals.

[10:53] Jenna Park: What’s the expected delta?

[10:56] Logan Wright: If all telemetry dimensions are complete, we aim for within 1–3% depending on backfill timing. The biggest drift historically is missing streaming output tokens or “unknown region” rows, which we now alert on.

[11:12] Allison Grant: Also timezone boundaries. Your finance runs PST close; pipeline rolls up hourly in UTC. We can align the report to your finance day boundary.

[11:23] Jenna Park: Yes, we close in PST.

[11:26] Sarah Kim: That explains why some days looked off by one.

[11:29] Aditya Rao: Okay. Now I’ll pull up the “Top drivers” table. This is top routes by cost contribution.

[11:38] Aditya Rao: Route one: clinical-chat. Route two: claim-summarize. Claim-summarize is the fast-growing one.

[11:48] Miguel Alvarez: That’s expected.

[11:50] Aditya Rao: On claim-summarize, average output length is stable, but input length increased 22% over the period.

[12:00] Dr. Priya Nair: That’s because we include longer claim history.

[12:03] Aditya Rao: Right. Optimization idea: compress history via embeddings or retrieval, or summarize the history first with a smaller model, then pass a shorter context to the big model.

[12:17] Sarah Kim: We have an internal retrieval system but it’s not integrated yet.

[12:20] Miguel Alvarez: We could do a two-stage pipeline. But complexity.

[12:25] Aditya Rao: Not a v1 requirement. Another simpler thing: truncate or structure the history more. Even moving from raw text to a table-like format can reduce tokens.

[12:37] Dr. Priya Nair: We can explore.

[12:39] Jenna Park: If you can quantify the expected savings, it helps me justify engineering work.

[12:44] Aditya Rao: Yep. That’s literally what this dashboard is for internally: quantify impact, find regressions, prioritize.

[12:52] Sarah Kim: Are we seeing any regressions you think are on your side? Not ours.

[12:56] Nadia Rahman: There was the streaming token metering issue, which is measurement not cost, but it’s on us. Cost-wise, we did not see a hardware rate increase in that window. There was a short ingestion lag incident that caused missing hours in the dashboard, but it should not affect billing.

[13:13] Sarah Kim: We saw a day with almost zero tokens in your chart.

[13:17] Allison Grant: Yeah that was the ingestion lag. We backfilled. We’re tightening SLOs and alerting around “missing hours.”

[13:25] Jenna Park: This is why Finance doesn’t trust dashboards.

[13:28] Aditya Rao: Understood. Our goal is to make it dependable enough for exec reporting, which means data quality gates.

[13:36] Sarah Kim: Okay.

[13:37] Aditya Rao: Let’s talk targets for next quarter. What’s your goal? Lower blended $/1M by X%? Or reduce variance?

[13:46] Jenna Park: Both. Ideally 10% improvement by end of Q2, but we can start with 5% and less surprises.

[13:54] Dr. Priya Nair: For me, we can’t trade off quality. We’re already tight on accuracy.

[14:00] Aditya Rao: Agreed. We’ll gate quantization experiments with evals and we won’t touch clinical assistant without explicit signoff.

[14:08] Miguel Alvarez: Can you show the difference between streaming and non-streaming cost? Like is streaming more expensive?

[14:14] Aditya Rao: Streaming itself doesn’t change compute; it changes how tokens are delivered. It can impact batching a bit depending on backpressure. In our dashboard, we can filter streaming=true and see if batching efficiency differs.

[14:28] Aditya Rao: Filtering… For clinical-chat, streaming requests have slightly lower batching efficiency, ~0.74 vs 0.78.

[14:37] Miguel Alvarez: Why?

[14:38] Aditya Rao: Because decode is longer-lived per request and can reduce batch packing efficiency. But the effect is small. Usually the UX gain is worth it.

[14:49] Dr. Priya Nair: We need streaming for the clinician experience.

[14:52] Aditya Rao: Great.

[14:53] Sarah Kim: What about cache in streaming mode?

[14:56] Aditya Rao: Cache hit rate is similar once the prefix is stable. The bigger factor is prompt variability.

[15:03] Sarah Kim: Okay.

[15:05] Aditya Rao: I want to pause and ask: do you have concerns about data residency or logging retention with these metrics? Because we’re talking about dashboards.

[15:13] Sarah Kim: Metrics are fine. We just don’t want request bodies logged.

[15:17] Allison Grant: We don’t store prompts in this pipeline. It’s aggregated counters and dimensions like model, region, tier, and flags like streaming. No customer IDs exposed in drilldowns.

[15:28] Jenna Park: Good.

[15:30] Aditya Rao: Okay, let’s outline a concrete plan:

[15:33] Aditya Rao: 1) Prompt stabilization to recover prefix cache hits. 2) Batch tuning in eu-west for the two routes. 3) Int8 quant experiment on claim-summarize with eval gate. 4) Monthly recon snapshot aligned to PST.

[15:50] Sarah Kim: That sounds right.

[15:51] Dr. Priya Nair: And I want an explicit review before anything changes for clinical assistant.

[15:56] Aditya Rao: Absolutely.

[15:58] Miguel Alvarez: For batch tuning, is that something you do or we do?

[16:01] Aditya Rao: Redwood will propose configs. We may need you to approve a maintenance window depending on how it’s deployed, but it’s low risk.

[16:10] Miguel Alvarez: Okay.

[16:11] Jenna Park: Can you explain “blended” again? I need to repeat it.

[16:15] Logan Wright: Blended includes: GPU compute cost allocated to your tier, plus shared overhead allocations (like control plane and some shared services) per a defined methodology. For Dedicated, we include idle capacity treatment based on reserved pool. So if you reserve capacity and don’t use it, some idle cost is included in blended.

[16:39] Jenna Park: That’s important. Are we paying for idle in the contract anyway?

[16:42] Logan Wright: Contract-wise you pay the commit, yes. So it’s consistent. The dashboard is trying to show the “true” cost basis.

[16:51] Sarah Kim: So if we increase min replicas, it could raise idle and blended.

[16:56] Aditya Rao: Correct. That’s why we model the net effect.

[17:01] Dr. Priya Nair: I’d rather have steady latency.

[17:04] Aditya Rao: Makes sense.

[17:05] (crosstalk)
[17:06] Sarah Kim: Sorry, can you show the idle component?

[17:08] Logan Wright: Internally we can break it out, yes. For external sharing we can give you a summary: utilized vs idle allocation. We just need to be careful with how we present it.

[17:20] Jenna Park: Please include it. Otherwise Finance assumes we’re getting “overcharged” when usage dips.

[17:26] Aditya Rao: Got it.

[17:28] Aditya Rao: Another thing: rate card updates. Our Finance updates quarterly. If the rate card changes, we version it and annotate. That might have contributed to some step changes you saw earlier in Q4.

[17:42] Jenna Park: We need a heads up. Even if it’s just “methodology changed.”

[17:46] Logan Wright: Agree. We can include it in monthly snapshot.

[17:50] Sarah Kim: Okay.

[17:52] Aditya Rao: Any questions on the dashboard drilldowns? Model, region, tier are the main ones.

[17:57] Miguel Alvarez: I’d love drilldown by model version and quant profile, but I know that might be more internal.

[18:03] Aditya Rao: We can share the results, not necessarily direct access.

[18:07] Sarah Kim: That’s fine.

[18:09] Dr. Priya Nair: For quantization: what kind of quality regressions do you typically see?

[18:14] Aditya Rao: For summarization, it can be subtle: missed entities, more repetition, slight factual drift. That’s why we use evals and sometimes human spot-checking for critical domains.

[18:27] Dr. Priya Nair: We can provide a rubric: ICD code accuracy, medication mentions, and no invented procedures.

[18:34] Aditya Rao: Perfect.

[18:36] Aditya Rao: Let’s do a quick recap of what happened in January, because I want to make sure we’re aligned:

[18:41] Aditya Rao: - You enabled streaming and changed prompts.
[18:44] Aditya Rao: - Output token metering for streaming had an undercount; we fixed it.
[18:48] Aditya Rao: - EU share increased; EU has higher GPU cost and lower utilization.
[18:53] Aditya Rao: - Cache hit rate dropped due to prompt variability.

[18:57] Sarah Kim: Yep.

[18:58] Jenna Park: That’s the story.

[19:00] Allison Grant: And we’ll set alerts so a missing-hours situation doesn’t linger.

[19:05] Sarah Kim: Great.

[19:07] Aditya Rao: Okay, we have about 30 minutes left. Do you want to go deeper on any one lever? Batching or caching or quantization.

[19:14] Miguel Alvarez: Caching. Specifically, how do we structure prompts to maximize prefix cache hits without making the prompt worse?

[19:21] Aditya Rao: Cool. The rule of thumb: stable prefix, variable suffix. The cache is keyed on the prefix tokens. So keep system prompt, safety policy, tool definitions, and common instructions identical. Put per-patient or per-department data later.

[19:38] Miguel Alvarez: Tool definitions are big. We’re sending them every time.

[19:42] Aditya Rao: If they’re identical, they cache well. If you reorder fields or include dynamic descriptions, it hurts.

[19:49] Sarah Kim: We do inject department names into tool descriptions.

[19:53] Aditya Rao: That’s likely the hit.

[19:55] Dr. Priya Nair: But the clinician needs to see the department.

[19:58] Miguel Alvarez: That’s not in tool definitions. That’s in the user-visible content.

[20:02] Aditya Rao: Right. Keep tool schemas generic; you can pass department in the user message.

[20:10] Miguel Alvarez: Okay.

[20:12] Aditya Rao: Also, for long histories, consider summarizing the history once and then reusing it across turns. That improves cache because the prefix stays consistent.

[20:24] Sarah Kim: That’s a product change but feasible.

[20:27] Jenna Park: Can you quantify what 34% to 19% cache hit means in dollars?

[20:33] Aditya Rao: Roughly, for your volume, it’s in the low thousands per month today. If we recover to 30%+ we’d expect a few percent reduction in blended $/1M for those routes, assuming other factors constant.

[20:47] Jenna Park: I’ll take it.

[20:49] Dr. Priya Nair: As long as we don’t degrade quality.

[20:52] Aditya Rao: Shouldn’t.

[20:54] Logan Wright: We can include this as a “driver estimate” in the recap.

[20:59] Aditya Rao: Great.

[21:01] Sarah Kim: Batching next. How risky is changing batching windows? We’re sensitive to p99 latency.

[21:08] Aditya Rao: We tune within guardrails. Usually we adjust max batch tokens and window by a few milliseconds. The goal is better throughput without affecting p99 too much. We can canary in eu-west only.

[21:22] Miguel Alvarez: We’ll want a rollback.

[21:24] Aditya Rao: Of course.

[21:26] Allison Grant: We can watch the latency SLOs and stop the rollout if p99 crosses threshold.

[21:33] Sarah Kim: Okay.

[21:34] Jenna Park: On the monthly recon snapshot: what do you need from us?

[21:39] Logan Wright: Confirm timezone and any invoice line items that shouldn’t be included in compute (support fees, etc.). We’ll isolate compute-like categories.

[21:51] Jenna Park: I’ll send the details.

[21:53] Aditya Rao: Perfect.

[21:55] Dr. Priya Nair: One question: you mentioned “tier” dimension. We’re Dedicated; what’s hosted burst in this context?

[22:02] Aditya Rao: When your dedicated pool is saturated, we route overflow to hosted capacity per policy. It’s rare for you but it happens during traffic spikes.

[22:12] Sarah Kim: Is hosted burst more expensive?

[22:15] Aditya Rao: Usually yes per token, but it protects availability. We can show how often it happens. It’s like 1–2% of tokens in this period.

[22:24] Sarah Kim: Not a big deal.

[22:26] Miguel Alvarez: We did have an outage risk during a campaign.

[22:28] Aditya Rao: Exactly.

[22:30] Aditya Rao: Okay, I’m going to stop sharing and summarize next steps.

[22:35] Aditya Rao: Nadia will send the streaming metering fix write-up with dates. Logan will send the monthly reconciliation snapshot proposal and align to PST. I’ll send recommended batching and caching adjustments for your two main routes and propose the int8 quant experiment plan.

[22:52] Sarah Kim: And we’ll send you eval prompts.

[22:54] Miguel Alvarez: And I’ll look at prompt stabilization: keep tool definitions static.

[22:59] Jenna Park: And I’ll confirm the PST close and what Finance wants in the report.

[23:05] Aditya Rao: Great.

[23:07] Dr. Priya Nair: Can we schedule the technical working session now?

[23:10] Aditya Rao: Sure. Sarah/Miguel, what’s good week of Feb 17?

[23:15] Sarah Kim: Tuesday 10am PST works.

[23:18] Aditya Rao: Done. We’ll send a calendar invite.

[23:22] Allison Grant: I’ll also loop in our oncall alias for alerts; we’ll ask who should get them on your side.

[23:30] Sarah Kim: Me and Miguel.

[23:32] Jenna Park: And maybe our FinOps email list.

[23:35] Allison Grant: Great.

[23:37] Aditya Rao: Anything else before we wrap?

[23:40] Jenna Park: Just—please make the “this was measurement change” super clear. Finance gets spooked.

[23:45] Nadia Rahman: Understood.

[23:47] Aditya Rao: Cool. Thanks everyone.

[23:50] (Meeting continues with light scheduling chatter and ends)
